Letter to the Editor iju_2520 587..588
Urodynamic study alterations in a patient with stiff
person syndrome
The stiff person syndrome (SPS) is characterized by a
group of symptoms that include muscular stiffness, spasms
of axial origin and generalized myalgias; this syndrome
was described for the ﬁrst time by Moersch in 1956.
1 In
1967, Gordon et al. described the diagnostic criteria that
made it possible to deﬁne this disease; 2 these criteria were
subsequently modiﬁed by Lorish et al. in 1989, and are
still in use today. 3 This syndrome, which has a primary
autoimmune origin, is characterized by the occurrence of
speciﬁc anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibod-
ies in comparison with the occurrence of the GAD-65
isoform that is present in the serum or cerebrospinal ﬂuid
in 60–80% of patients, and its etiology is unknown. It
seems that this antibody-mediated reaction triggers alter-
ations on the gamma-Aminobutyric acid system that would
directly be involved with the appearance of uninhibited
continuous muscular activity, and also with the patient’s
phobias. Despite the progress achieved in the diagnosis of
this condition, it is on many occasions diagnosed too late
and when it has already left after-effects on patients. The
prognosis is poor, as a result of the syndrome progressing
to total disability over time, and even sudden death can
occur by autonomic dysfunction. The ideal treatment is
diazepam, but valproic acid , clonidine, vigabatrin and even
botulinum toxin can also be used. In more severe cases,
steroids, immunoglobulin and plasmapheresis are used.
4
Our objective is to show in a detailed way the alterations
found in a urodynamic study that was carried out in patients
diagnosed with SPS.
W e describe the case of a 45 year-old female patient, who
over 5 years suffered from painful cramps in the lower and
upper limbs, she had difﬁculty in walking, showed hyperre-
ﬂexia, and an electromyogram showed continuous muscular
activity; she was diagnosed with SPS at the neurology
department and was referred to our urology service for a
urodynamic study because the patient showed difﬁculty in
passing urine, there was a delay in the initiation of micturi-
tion, a weak urinary stream and the sensation of incomplete
emptying after micturition. The patient underwent the afore-
mentioned urodynamic study, which included the following
remarkable alterations:
• Flowmetry: Broken and low micturition ﬂow (Qmax,
6 mL/s) and signiﬁcant post-urinary residues (Fig. 1.1).
• Bladder-ﬁlling cystomanometry: Bladder capacity was
somewhat diminished and showed normal bladder
accommodation and absence of detrusor waves.
• Bladder-emptying cystomanometry through surface
electromyography: Signiﬁcant delay in the initiation of
micturition, low and broken urine ﬂow, and a signiﬁcant
increase of detrusor pressure. Apart from these ﬁndings,
an increased activity of the striated sphincter was also
observed , which reached up to 250 micro-volts
(Fig. 1.2).
Therefore, this condition comprises a detrusor-sphincter
dyssynergia caused by an increment in the activity of the
striated sphincter muscle. The patient was treated with
muscle relaxants, but she left the treatment feeling drowsy,
so she was treated with corticosteroids and she had the same
urinary symptoms.
W e consequently believe that the present urodynamic
study is a useful trial that illustrates the precise urinary
alterations found in patients afﬂicted with SPS, and shows

that it is possible to treat this condition with muscle-
relaxants.
Miguel Angel Arrabal-Polo
MD, Francisco Palao-Y ago MD
and Armando Zuluaga-Gomez MD
Urology Department, University of Granada,
San Cecilio University Hospital, Granada, Spain
arrabalp@ono.com
